newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU faces explosion in allergies - report.
newsitem.headline: EU faces explosion in allergies - report.

text.p: One in two people in the European Union will suffer from an allergy soon unless preventive action is taken urgently, the head of the British-based UCB Institute of Allergy warned on Wednesday.
"The number of people with allergies, especially children, doubles every 10 years. Soon one in two people will be affected," secretary-general Anne Wilmes told Reuters.

She was speaking before the presentation to the European Parliament on Wednesday of the first European White Paper on Allergy, which describes the problem and recommends action "to stem and repulse the allergenic invasion of Europe".

According to the 120-page report, which is based on the research of 21 leading European allergists, one in three Europeans now suffer from allergies ranging from asthma, hay fever, allergies to house dust and pets, dermatitis, intolerance to foods (especially milk, eggs and peanuts) and drugs.

The report warns that the situation is worsening: "In some regions about half of all children and young people are now affected with allergy -- and we do not know the potential size of the susceptible population".

"The situation is becoming dramatic," Wilmes said, adding that the problem was compounded by inadequate medical diagnosis and treatment and led to rising costs to society, in terms of overstretched public health systems and loss of workdays.
"It is estimated that the yearly direct and indirect costs of allergies in Europe amount to 29 billion ecus ($43 billion)," the report says.
The causes of allergies are complex and more research will be needed but a number of causal factors have already been identified, Wilmes said.

Much of the problem lies with the lifestyle adopted in industrialised countries: houses with carpets, pets, gas cookers and poor ventilation; increasing contact with chemicals and industrially processed foods; a drop in breast-feeding, which is one of the most crucial ways of developing the infant's immune system; certain vaccines and smoking.

Wilmes said an accusing finger had often been pointed at car and industrial pollution but studies comparing eastern and western Europe at the time of the fall of the Berlin Wall showed that in spite of their dire air pollution problems, the east European countries had a much lower incidence of allergies than their more developed western neighbours.

The Institute of Allergy report, welcomed by EU Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn as a way of raising awareness and provoking debate, calls for a European Allergy Prevention Programme which would bring all EU countries up to the standards of the Scandinavians.

This includes preventive action by individuals, such as "breast-feeding during the first months of life, improved ventilation in houses, avoidance of pets (also in day-care centres and schools), avoidance of smoking and passive exposure during pregnancy".

But it also proposed measures for the authorities, ranging from a total ban on smoking in public places and effective public information campaigns, to more funding for research and medical training and the introduction of international standards for allergenic preparations.

Wilmes said she wanted governments to go even further and adopt Swedish-style social security systems which allow mothers to breast feed for longer by giving them six months parental leave and, in places like Finland where gas is widely used as a domestic fuel, switch to other sources of heat and power.
But she insisted: "We are not here to give orders. We're just here to say it is a big problem and everyone should be aware of it."
